explanations.answer: Take as wives whomever they choose
explanations.explanation: You got it, baker. The text says the sons of God saw that the daughters of men were beautiful, and "…they took as wives whomever they chose." Notice the choosing was all theirs. The passage doesn't say anyone else got a vote.

explanations.answer: Wait for the LORD to choose for them
explanations.explanation: Good thinking, friend, but the text goes another way. Nothing in these verses says they waited on anybody. It says "…they took as wives whomever they chose." The choosing was theirs.

explanations.answer: Ask the fathers for their permission
explanations.explanation: I get why you'd pick that, friend. It sounds like the polite thing to do. But the text never mentions anyone being asked. It just says "…they took as wives whomever they chose." The passage stays quiet about permission, so I will too.

That's the number, baker. The LORD says, "My Spirit will not contend with man forever, for he is mortal; his days shall be 120 years." Just a few verses back, Methuselah, Enoch's son, lived 969 years (Genesis 5:27). So 120 is a number you notice right after all those long ones. The verse doesn't say more than what the LORD says here, so I'll leave it right there.
Close enough to make me squint, friend. But the LORD gives a different number in this verse. He says, "his days shall be 120 years." That's what the text says, so that's the number I'm baking with.
I see you going small there, friend. But the LORD names a bigger number than that. He says, "his days shall be 120 years." That's the number in this verse, so that's the one that stays.

That's the word, baker. "Then the LORD saw that the wickedness of man was great upon the earth…" (Genesis 6:5). The verse keeps going and says every inclination of the thoughts of his heart was altogether evil all the time. I think this is one of the hard spots in the passage. The LORD sees all of it, and I'd rather read it slowly than rush past it.

Nice word, friend, but it isn't the one in the verse. The text says the LORD saw that the wickedness of man was great upon the earth. That's a heavy thing to read. Wisdom is a good word, but it's not what the LORD sees here.
I wish that was the word, friend. But the text says the LORD saw that the wickedness of man was great upon the earth. This is a heavy part of the passage. The verse just says it straight.

I can see why you'd pick that, friend, but the text says more than that. It says "…every inclination of the thoughts of his heart was altogether evil all the time." All the time, not just some of it. So the answer here is False.

You read it right, baker. The text says "…every inclination of the thoughts of his heart was altogether evil all the time." Not some of the time, all the time. So False is the one that matches the verse.

That's right, baker. The text says, "…the LORD regretted that He had made man on the earth, and He was grieved in His heart." Both parts are right there in the same verse. This one hurts to read, so I'll just let it sit for a moment.

Not this time, friend. The verse says, "…the LORD regretted that He had made man on the earth, and He was grieved in His heart." So the grief is in the text, right next to the regret. I think this verse is meant to be read slowly.

explanations.answer: Blot out man from the earth
explanations.explanation: That's right, baker. The LORD says, "I will blot out man, whom I have created, from the face of the earth…" (Genesis 6:7). Then He adds that He is grieved that He made them. I think that's the part to sit with. The text says He was grieved in His heart (Genesis 6:6), and that makes this verse hit harder.

I see where that comes from, friend. Man was sent away from the Garden of Eden once before (Genesis 3:23). But that's not what the LORD says here. He says, "I will blot out man, whom I have created, from the face of the earth…"

That's a real thing in the Bible, friend, just not here. Later, the LORD scattered people from a city over all the earth (Genesis 11:8). In this verse the LORD says something different: "I will blot out man, whom I have created, from the face of the earth…" That's what the text says here.
Yes, baker. The LORD says, "…every man and beast and crawling creature and bird of the air…" The list goes past man to the animals too. It's a long list, and the verse doesn't hurry through it.

Good try, friend, but the verse gives a longer list. The LORD says, "…every man and beast and crawling creature and bird of the air…" So the beasts and the birds are named right there in what He says. The text spells it out.
That's him, baker. "Noah, however, found favor in the eyes of the LORD." That little word "however" turns the whole verse around. After all that heavy news, here's one man the text sets apart.

Methuselah, Enoch's son, is a fun guess, friend. He lived 969 years, longer than anyone else in the list, and then he died. But the verse about favor names someone else: "Noah, however, found favor in the eyes of the LORD." So the longest life doesn't win here.
Jared, Enoch's father, is in the family line, friend. He lived 962 years and then he died. But he isn't the one this verse names. It says, "Noah, however, found favor in the eyes of the LORD."
